Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-2-prompt-long-0135", "row_sha256": "8d94f0c9cea69c864b688347faa3e1be6e920bb9457e11f630ed9a021a431c47", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you make this into one standalone fictional update about a screen reader audit, not a general accessibility explainer. set it at the fictional North Quay Library and make the episode about the online room booking form that the library uses for its two study rooms. it should read like a normal internal update that a project team might actually circulate, with connected paragraphs and enough concrete detail that someone who was not at the audit can follow what happened. please don't turn it into a victory story or make the audit sound bigger than it was. the team checked the booking form and its immediate confirmation step, not the whole library website, the library app, or the in-person booking process.

the audit was on 14 May, with Mara Chen from the library digital team and Joel Price, an accessibility tester contracted for this review. they used a Windows laptop with NVDA and Firefox. say that plainly; don't suggest they also tested other browsers, devices, or screen readers. they went through the form using the keyboard and screen reader, and checked the confirmation page after a test booking. the test was done in the staging site, so nothing was reserved in the live room calendar. the audit took about an hour and a half, and the library's web developer, Imani Cole, joined for the final twenty minutes by video call. maybe mention she was there to hear the findings, but don't say she fixed anything during the session.

a useful detail is that the date field was announced as “Choose a date” but its error message, when they left it blank and tried to continue, was not announced automatically. Joel found it only after moving back through the page with the screen reader. include both halves of that finding, since the field label itself was available and the problem was with how the error was announced. don't rewrite it as if the form had no date label at all. another finding: the room choices were radio buttons and their names, “Harbour Room” and “Map Room,” were read correctly, but the capacity note beside each option was not included in the radio button's accessible name. the capacity notes say “up to 8 people” for Harbour Room and “up to 4 people” for Map Room. users could still hear those notes by moving through the nearby text, so the issue was that the information wasn't associated with each choice, not that it was missing from the page.

there was one more keyboard issue on the confirmation step. after a test booking, the page displayed a heading saying “Request received,” but focus stayed at the top of the page rather than moving to that heading. the heading could be found by navigating through the page. be careful to keep those facts together and don't claim a booking email was tested; the audit didn't check email notifications. Joel also noted that the form's required-field instructions were available before the fields, and that keyboard focus was visible around the Continue and Submit buttons. those things worked in this session, so include them as observed strengths without turning that into a claim that every control worked.

please include a plain account of what the people agreed at the end. Mara asked Imani to log the three findings in the team's issue tracker. Imani said she would check whether the date error and confirmation focus could be handled in the next maintenance release, but no commitment or release date was set. the radio-button capacity association needs a separate review with the form vendor, because the library staff cannot change that part themselves. nobody decided on a launch delay, and the audit did not establish whether any changes have since been made. keep these as next steps and open items, not completed fixes or approvals.

maybe use a short numbered section if it helps make the three findings easy to scan, but keep the rest in ordinary prose, not a wall of bullets. include an ordinary reported quote from the meeting: Mara said, “We can track these separately and come back with an update after the vendor review.” don't add a new speaker or a second quote, and don't imply that this update has already happened. there should be a clear final section or final paragraph that gives the current assessment and what remains unresolved. that ending needs to preserve the actual scope: this was a limited check of the booking form in staging with NVDA and Firefox, and the team has findings to follow up, but it hasn't assessed other assistive technologies or the rest of the service. don't finish with a made-up recommendation or a broad statement that the library is accessible or inaccessible.

keep the update self-contained and use the names and details above accurately. spread concrete details through the piece instead of repeating the same conclusion in every paragraph. don't invent extra test results, fixes, dates, people, user impact, or decisions. keep the uncertainty around the possible maintenance-release work, and distinguish what was observed from what still needs checking. i want a complete, natural update with a distinct ending, not a summary pasted on after it.", "output": "Write one self-contained, fictional internal update about a screen-reader audit at North Quay Library. Focus only on the online room booking form for the library’s two study rooms and its immediate confirmation step. Do not present it as a general accessibility explainer or as a victory story. Write connected, substantive paragraphs that make sense to readers who were not at the audit. A short numbered section may be used to make the findings easy to scan, but keep the rest in ordinary prose rather than turning the update into a wall of bullets.

The audit took place on 14 May. Mara Chen from the library digital team and Joel Price, an accessibility tester contracted for this review, tested the form on a Windows laptop using NVDA and Firefox. They used the keyboard and screen reader, then checked the confirmation page after a test booking. Testing took place on the staging site, so nothing was reserved in the live room calendar. The session lasted about an hour and a half. The library’s web developer, Imani Cole, joined by video call for the final twenty minutes to hear the findings; do not say that she fixed anything during the session. Do not imply that other browsers, devices, or screen readers were tested.

Describe these three findings accurately:

1. The date field was announced as “Choose a date.” When the testers left it blank and tried to continue, its error message was not announced automatically. Joel found the message only after moving back through the page with the screen reader. The field label was available; the issue was the announcement of the error, not a missing date label.
2. The room choices were radio buttons, and their names, “Harbour Room” and “Map Room,” were read correctly. The capacity note beside each option was not included in that radio button’s accessible name. The notes read “up to 8 people” for Harbour Room and “up to 4 people” for Map Room. Users could still hear the notes by moving through nearby text, so describe the problem as a lack of association with each choice, not as missing information from the page.
3. On the confirmation step after a test booking, the page displayed the heading “Request received,” but focus remained at the top of the page instead of moving to the heading. The heading could be found by navigating through the page. The audit did not check email notifications, so make no claim about a booking email.

Also report the observed strengths without overstating them: required-field instructions were available before the fields, and keyboard focus was visible around the Continue and Submit buttons. These observations do not establish that every control worked.

Explain what was agreed at the end of the session. Mara asked Imani to log the three findings in the team’s issue tracker. Imani said she would check whether the date error and confirmation focus could be handled in the next maintenance release, but there was no commitment or release date. The radio-button capacity association needs a separate review with the form vendor because library staff cannot change that part themselves. No one decided on a launch delay, and the audit did not establish whether any changes have since been made. Present these as next steps and open items, not completed fixes or approvals.

Include this single ordinary reported quote from the meeting: Mara said, “We can track these separately and come back with an update after the vendor review.” Do not add another quote or speaker, or imply that the promised update has already happened.

End with a distinct final section or paragraph stating the current assessment and what remains unresolved. Preserve the audit’s limited scope: it was a check of the booking form in staging using NVDA and Firefox, and the team has findings to follow up. The audit did not assess other assistive technologies or the rest of the service. Do not claim that the whole library service is accessible or inaccessible, and do not add a recommendation. Keep observations distinct from matters still to be checked, retain the uncertainty about possible maintenance-release work, and do not invent test results, fixes, dates, people, user impact, or decisions. Make the update complete and natural, with concrete details distributed throughout rather than repeated conclusions."}]
